title: Lists & Tuples
description: Store, organize, and manipulate ordered collections of data

lessons.title: Lists Basics
lessons.description: Create and access Python's most-used data structure

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Create lists, access/update elements, and check length.

sections.title: 📋 Creating & Accessing Lists
sections.content:
A list is an ordered, mutable collection.

```python
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
fruits[0]     # 'apple'
fruits[-1]    # 'cherry'
len(fruits)   # 3
```

sections.title: ✏️ Modifying Lists
sections.content:
Unlike strings, lists CAN be changed in place.

```python
fruits[1] = "blueberry"   # replace an item
fruits.append("date")     # add to the end
fruits.insert(0, "kiwi")  # insert at position
fruits.remove("apple")    # remove by value
fruits.pop()               # remove & return last item
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Confusing `remove(value)` (removes by value) with `pop(index)` (removes by position).

questions.question: How do you create an empty list?
questions.explanation: Square brackets create a list literal.

questions.question: Are Python lists mutable?
questions.explanation: You can change, add, or remove elements after creation.

questions.question: What does `fruits.append(x)` do?
questions.explanation: append adds a single item to the end.

questions.question: What does `fruits.remove('apple')` do?
questions.explanation: remove() searches by value, not position.

questions.question: What does `fruits.pop()` do by default?
options: Removes and returns the last item
questions.explanation: pop() without an argument removes the last element.

questions.question: How do you get the number of items in a list?
questions.explanation: len() works on all sequence types.

questions.question: What does `fruits.insert(0, 'kiwi')` do?
questions.explanation: insert(index, value) places the value at that position.

questions.question: What is `fruits[-1]`?
questions.explanation: Negative indexing counts from the end.

lessons.title: List Methods
lessons.description: Sort, search, and combine lists using built-in methods

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Sort, reverse, count, and search within lists.

sections.title: 🔃 Sorting
sections.content:
```python
nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
nums.sort()             # in place: [1, 1, 3, 4, 5]
nums.sort(reverse=True) # [5, 4, 3, 1, 1]

sorted([3, 1, 2])       # returns a NEW sorted list, original unchanged
```

sections.title: 🔍 Searching & Counting
sections.content:
```python
nums = [1, 2, 2, 3]
nums.count(2)     # 2 (how many times 2 appears)
2 in nums          # True
nums.index(3)      # 2 (position of first match)
```

sections.title: ➕ Combining Lists
sections.content:
```python
a = [1, 2]
b = [3, 4]
a + b            # [1, 2, 3, 4] (new list)
a.extend(b)      # a becomes [1, 2, 3, 4] (in place)
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Using `.sort()` (in place, returns None) when you meant `sorted()` (returns a new list) — `x = nums.sort()` sets x to None.

questions.question: What does `.sort()` return?
questions.explanation: sort() mutates the list and returns None.

questions.question: What does `sorted([3,1,2])` return?
options: A new sorted list, original unchanged
questions.explanation: sorted() is a builtin function returning a new list.

questions.question: What does `nums.count(2)` do?
questions.explanation: count() tallies matching elements.

questions.question: `a.extend(b)` does what to a?
options: Appends all items of b onto a in place
Adds b as a single nested item
questions.explanation: extend() adds each element of b individually.

questions.question: What does `a + b` do for two lists?
questions.explanation: + on lists concatenates, unlike NumPy arrays.

questions.question: `nums.index(3)` returns...
questions.explanation: index() finds the position of the first matching value.

questions.question: What is a common bug with `.sort()`?
options: Assigning its return value, which is None
questions.explanation: sort() modifies in place and returns None, unlike sorted().

questions.question: `nums.sort(reverse=True)` sorts...
questions.explanation: reverse=True flips the sort order.

lessons.title: List Slicing & Comprehensions
lessons.description: Extract sublists and build lists in one line

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Slice lists like strings, and write basic list comprehensions.

sections.title: ✂️ Slicing Lists
sections.content:
Slicing works exactly like strings.

```python
nums = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
nums[1:4]    # [1, 2, 3]
nums[:3]     # [0, 1, 2]
nums[::2]    # [0, 2, 4]
nums[::-1]   # [5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0]
```

sections.title: ⚡ List Comprehensions
sections.content:
A compact way to build a new list from an existing iterable.

```python
squares = [x**2 for x in range(5)]
# [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]

evens = [x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
# [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
```

This replaces a longer loop:
```python
squares = []
for x in range(5):
    squares.append(x**2)
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Writing comprehensions so complex they become unreadable — if it needs more than one condition/loop, a regular for loop is often clearer.

questions.question: What does `[x**2 for x in range(3)]` produce?
questions.explanation: Squares of 0, 1, 2.

questions.question: What does `[x for x in range(6) if x % 2 == 0]` produce?
questions.explanation: Filters for even numbers only.

questions.question: What is `nums[1:4]` on `[0,1,2,3,4,5]`?
questions.explanation: Slice from index 1 up to (not including) 4.

questions.question: A list comprehension is equivalent to...
options: A for loop building a new list
questions.explanation: It's syntactic sugar for a simple building loop.

questions.question: What does `nums[::-1]` do to a list?
questions.explanation: Negative step -1 walks backward through the list.

questions.question: When should you avoid a list comprehension?
options: When it becomes too complex to read easily
questions.explanation: Readability should guide the choice between comprehension and loop.

questions.question: What is `[x for x in range(3)]`?
questions.explanation: Simple pass-through comprehension over range(3).

questions.question: Slicing a list returns...
questions.explanation: Slicing always creates a new list object.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Create tuples, understand immutability, and unpack them.

sections.title: 📦 Creating Tuples
sections.content:
Tuples look like lists but use parentheses and can't be changed after creation.

```python
point = (3, 4)
single = (5,)   # comma required for a one-item tuple!
empty = ()

point[0]   # 3
len(point) # 2
```

sections.title: 🔒 Why Use Tuples?
sections.content:
Tuples are immutable — great for fixed data (coordinates, RGB values) and can be used as dictionary keys, unlike lists.

```python
colors = {(255, 0, 0): "red", (0, 255, 0): "green"}
```

sections.title: 📤 Unpacking
sections.content:
```python
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x, y)   # 3 4
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting the trailing comma for a single-element tuple — `(5)` is just the int 5, not a tuple.

questions.question: How do you write a tuple with one item, 5?
questions.explanation: A trailing comma is required to distinguish it from parentheses used for grouping.

questions.question: Are tuples mutable?
questions.explanation: Once created, a tuple's contents cannot change.

questions.question: Can tuples be used as dictionary keys?
questions.explanation: Immutable, hashable types like tuples can be dict keys.

questions.question: What does `x, y = (3, 4)` do?
options: Unpacks 3 into x and 4 into y
Sets x and y both to (3,4)
questions.explanation: Tuple unpacking assigns each element to a name.

questions.question: What is `()`?
questions.explanation: Empty parentheses create an empty tuple.

questions.question: A key difference between lists and tuples is...
options: Tuples are immutable, lists are mutable
questions.explanation: Mutability is the primary distinguishing feature.

questions.question: What does `len((1,2,3))` return?
questions.explanation: len() counts the elements just like a list.

questions.question: Why might you choose a tuple over a list?
options: To signal the data shouldn't change, and to use as a dict key
Tuples are always faster to sort
questions.explanation: Immutability communicates intent and enables hashability.

lessons.title: Nested Lists
lessons.description: Work with lists inside lists (2D data)

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Access and loop through nested lists (e.g., grids or matrices).

sections.title: 🔁 Looping Through Nested Lists
sections.content:
```python
for row in matrix:
    for value in row:
        print(value, end=" ")
    print()  # newline after each row
```

A nested list comprehension can flatten a matrix:
```python
flat = [value for row in matrix for value in row]
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Copying a nested list with `list(matrix)` — this only makes a shallow copy, so inner lists are still shared. Use `copy.deepcopy()` for a true independent copy.

questions.question: What does `matrix[0][1]` mean?
questions.explanation: First index selects the row, second selects the column within it.

questions.question: What does a nested for loop over a matrix let you do?
options: Visit every value, row by row
questions.explanation: Outer loop picks a row, inner loop walks its values.

questions.question: Does `list(matrix)` deep copy nested lists?
questions.explanation: Inner lists remain shared references after a shallow copy.

questions.question: What module helps make a true independent copy of nested data?
questions.explanation: copy.deepcopy() recursively copies nested structures.

questions.question: What does `[v for row in matrix for v in row]` do?
options: Flattens the matrix into one list
questions.explanation: This is a nested comprehension that flattens 2D data.

questions.question: How many elements does a 3x3 matrix have?
questions.explanation: 3 rows times 3 columns = 9 elements.

questions.question: What is `matrix[2]` in the example matrix?
questions.explanation: Row index 2 is the third row.

questions.question: Nested lists are commonly used to represent...
questions.explanation: 2D data structures naturally map to lists of lists.
